newsitem.title: USA: Some issuers using problem SLGS provision - NABL.
newsitem.headline: Some issuers using problem SLGS provision - NABL.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury Department may already be too late to prevent some investment banks from tapping a possible loophole in the agency's revised state and local government series (SLGS) program, a spokesman for a municipal bond lawyers group said.

"There are various banks that have been recommending this to clients," Amy Dunbar, director of governmental affairs for the National Association of Bond Lawyers (NABL), said in a telephone interview with Reuters on Tuesday.
Asked whether any localities have actually done such a deal, Dunbar said, "Yes. I don't know who."
NABL is one of nine groups that warned Treasury in a two-page letter Tuesday that a provision in final SLGS rules issued Oct. 21 could lead to "unintended use" by the market.

Specifically, the rules reduce significantly the time periods for subscribing to and cancelling SLGS orders and eliminate a requirement that SLGS cancellations be based on "cause," the groups pointed out.

As a result, there is no penalty attached to subscribing for SLGS up to 60 days prior to a scheduled delivery date, and then canceling the subscription within five to seven days of the scheduled delivery date, they said.
"This allows the SLGS program to be used to create an 'option' or 'hedge' on interest rates, with no penalty to the SLGS subscriber," the groups warned.
They said Treasury could address the problem by simply invoking a section of SLGS rules that authorizes the department's secretary to refuse an SLGS application.
Dunbar said groups decided to alert Treasury before a number of localities use the questioned provision.
"It is something we think is about to break as a cost-free hedge," Dunbar said.

"Therefore, we wanted to make sure that Treasury reviewed it and took its position before a lot of transactions got out the door," Dunbar said, noting that groups want to head off Treasury having to make "retroactive changes" in the new rule.
"We wanted to be open and above board with them and the market so that people were on notice that this had been called to Treasury's attention," she said.
The eight market groups that signed Tuesday's letter to Treasury worked closely with the department in developing the revised SLGS rules.
"We don't think (the provision) was in in the spirit of the cooperative relationship we had. We want to make sure that the working arrangement continues," Dunbar said.
